To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
The serum concentrations of all BFRs except TriBP have increased over the last two decades.

The serum concentrations of the polybrominated flame retardant (PBBR) compounds 2,2’,4,4’,5,5’-pentabromodiphe-nyl ether (BDE153) and 2,4’,4-tribromodipheny ether (BDE28) were higher in the serum samples from infants (0-1 years of age) compared to the serum samples from other groups.
The levels of brominated flame retardant (BFR) in human serum increased during the period 1980-1999, with the exception of the tri-brominated phenol (TBP).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the temporal trends and the influence of age and sex on serum levels of BFRs in the general Norwegian population.
the temporal trends and age and gender differences in human exposure to selected brominated flame-retardants in Norway.
the temporal trends in human serum concentrations of BDE-28, BDE-47, BDE-99, BDE-100, BDE-153, BDE-154, TriBP, and TBBP-A, as well as the role of age and gender.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the BFR levels in serum from Norway have been increasing during the period 1960 to 2000.
the exposure to BFR has increased during the last 20 years and that the body burden is independent of age, with the exception of infants.
the BFR concentrations are higher in the present generation than in the previous generation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that the BDEs and TriBP are persistent compounds, and their serum levels have increased during the past 20 years, while TBBP-A has not been used in Norway.
the BFR levels in the serum from Norwegians increased during the period from 1977 to the end of the 1990's and that infants (0- 4 years old) seem to experience elevated BFR exposure.
the exposure of the population in the period 1990-1999 to the sum of six PBDE congeners was 3 times higher than the exposure during the period 1980-1989.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the BDEs and other BFRs have been increasing over the last 20 years in Norwegian serum.
the BFRs are persistent in the human body and that exposure to BFR is not related to age.
the levels of BFRs in the human serum have been increasing since 1977, and that the levels are highest in the age group 4-9 years, indicating a high exposure of infants.
